output:
*Interview with Dr Casimir Vauthier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Thank you for waiting, Doctor. Let us take the evening in order. You dined here?

DR VAUTHIER: I did, Inspector. I have dined at this table for thirty years, more or less, and Aurèle keeps the custom of the year's end as carefully as he keeps his escapements.

MATTHEY: What happened at dinner, when the temple bell struck nine?

DR VAUTHIER: Aurèle asked us all to show him our watches. He does it every year. It is his joke and his tyranny. We held them out like schoolboys, and he looked at each one as though it had personally offended him. Mine was two minutes ahead of the bell. I showed him, and he grunted, which from Aurèle is a considerable concession.

MATTHEY: And afterwards?

DR VAUTHIER: Madame and I sat down to piquet in the salon. Odile plays a hard game, Inspector, and a cold one, and I lost more than a man of my age should lose to his old friend's wife. We played until a quarter to eleven by my watch.

MATTHEY: What happened then?

DR VAUTHIER: I wanted my cigar case, which was in my coat in the hall. So I got up and went out to fetch it. Odile began to play the piano as I went out. She plays Chopin, you know, and she plays him better than anyone in the canton, which is not a compliment I offer lightly.

MATTHEY: Did she stop?

DR VAUTHIER: She stopped when I came back.

MATTHEY: And then?

DR VAUTHIER: I sat down again, and the hall clock struck eleven a moment after I did. The old Morbier. It strikes by its own face, and one learns to listen to it as one listens to a difficult patient.

MATTHEY: Did you take up the game again?

DR VAUTHIER: We did, and I lost again. I cannot tell you more about the hour than that, Inspector, and I would not wish to pretend to. A man who has been playing cards does not keep count of the clocks.

MATTHEY: You examined Aurèle's body.

DR VAUTHIER: I did, when I was called to him. A blow to the back of the head. One heavy stroke, from behind. I would say he knew very little of it, and that death would have been very quick. That is a physician's opinion and I will stand by it. What I cannot give you is an hour of death. Anyone who offers you one from a body alone is selling you a watch that does not run.

MATTHEY: You attended Jules Monnier in his last illness.

DR VAUTHIER: In 1889. A dreadful business. Jules was Aurèle's younger brother and he bore his illness with a bad grace and a good deal of brandy. I sat with him at the end, and I have not forgotten the room. Félix was a boy then, and he has never quite forgiven the illness for taking his father, nor the doctor for failing to prevent it.

MATTHEY: Is there anything about the atelier you would like to tell me?

DR VAUTHIER: Only that the regulator stopped with its master. I know it is sentimental, Inspector, and I am not a sentimental man, but there it is. Tempus edax rerum. Time devours all things, and this year it has been very hungry.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Doctor. You have been very clear.

DR VAUTHIER: I have been clear for thirty years, Inspector. It is the only virtue my patients have ever allowed me. Would you care for a cigar? I have one left in the case, which I was lucky enough to fetch.
